chunks.text: petition, and we have five minutes set down for you to speak to that this afternoon. I'll hand over to you. Sounds good. Thank you. I'm an Iranian Kiwi and a member of Free Iran Unity New Zealand, the group that led this petition. We recognize that there's no established precedent for an opposition leader to address the parliament, and we are truly grateful for this opportunity.

However, there's clear international precedent for this kind of engagement. This year alone, Prince Reza Pahlavi has addressed Sweden's parliament and met with politicians and parliament members in Italy, Germany, US, Netherlands, UK, France, Ukraine, Canada, and has recently been invited to visit Australia.

More than 13,000 people have signed this petition, asking the parliament to invite Prince Reza Pahlavi. We're not asking parliament to support a particular political system or to decide Iran's future. That decision belongs to the Iranian people. We're simply asking parliament to listen.

For 47 years, the Iranian people have lived under a regime that has restricted basic freedoms, suppressed opposition, and violated fundamental human rights. In January 2026, millions of Iranians across more than 200 cities responded to calls for unity and change.

The regime responded with an internet blackout, unprecedented massacre, and mass repression. Prince Reza Pahlavi's name has been chanted on the streets of Iran, and he has become the most prominent opposition figure advocating for democratic change in the country.

What happens in Iran also matters to New Zealand, education, nationality, and security trade through the Hormuz and cost of living, and it also matters a lot to New Zealand's Iranian community. An address would give our elect representatives the opportunity to hear directly from Iran's opposition leader, understand the situation in Iran, and the possible pathways ahead.

Ultimately, this is about listening to those whose voices have been silenced. It's about human rights, and it's about democracy. It's about giving New Zealand the opportunity to hear directly from Iranians about a future that belongs to them. Thank you.

Very good. Question, Simon Court. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you, Sana. Thank you, Sherry and Rosa, and all of you who have made such an effort to raise the plight of the Iranian people with leaders in New Zealand. I have a question for you about what matters the Crown Prince raised in his recent engagements with political leaders that you think are important for New Zealand parliamentarians to know.

And did any of that cover the actions of the Iranian government against its people? Yes, absolutely. So the Crown Prince has been going around and talking to politicians about what is happening in Iran to the people, about everyday executions that are going on, about the massacre that happened in January, and the world mostly remained silent. But also about the future, about how the future will look like, what the plan is, what the prosperity project for Iran looks like, the framework that they have worked on to move Iran

post-Islamic regime, and for basically transition towards a democratic, secular community. And also forming connections and collaborations with other countries and how the outlook will look like with a free Iran. So just for the supplementary, Mr. Chair.

Did the Crown Prince suggest in any of his presentations to other parliaments or bodies what democratic countries could do to support the people of Iran? Yes. I think the most important thing that the democratic countries can do is to recognize the will and wish of the Iranian people for change, and their wish to get rid of the Islamic regime in Iran as the first step. To recognize that there is a legitimate opposition and opposition leader that the people of Iran are largely behind,

and support to go through the transition period post the Islamic regime. So yeah, if the international community can offer that recognition, and that is one of the things that the Crown Prince has been asking for, would help the Iranians in their fights greatly.

Right. Question from Honorable Damien O'Connor. Look, thank you very much. I'm just wondering, do you think that the recent conflict has helped the Iranian people or not? Recent conflict? Yes. So what's happening is there is a killing machine in Iran. In January, eighth and ninth of January, tens of thousands of people have been massacred by the regime. The recent conflict made the ground level for Iranian people by disarming the killing machine. Yes, it helped the Iranian people by saving more lives. If those conflict wouldn't have been placed,

certainly there would be hundreds of thousands of Iranian people would have been massacred by this regime. Thank you. All right. Thank you very much for your time today. Really appreciate you sending the petition first of all, and then speaking to it today. Thank you very much.
